paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Your body contains roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, most of them in the gut. Collectively known as the microbiome, these organisms help digest food, train the immune system and produce vitamins. Over the past two decades, research on the microbiome has expanded dramatically, with claims linking it to conditions as varied as obesity, depression, autism and cancer. The enthusiasm is understandable, but it has sometimes outrun the evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence concerns infection. In a condition caused by the bacterium Clostridioides difficile, which flourishes when antibiotics have killed rival gut bacteria, patients can suffer repeated, sometimes fatal, diarrhoea. Transplanting stool from a healthy donor restores a balanced community, and in trials it cured around nine in ten patients, a far higher rate than antibiotics. That result persuaded many sceptics that manipulating the microbiome can have real clinical value.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For most other conditions, the picture is much less clear. Studies in mice show that transferring gut bacteria from obese animals to lean ones can cause weight gain, but such effects have been hard to reproduce in humans. A frequent difficulty is distinguishing cause from consequence: does an unusual microbiome contribute to a disease, or does the disease, through changes in diet or medication, alter the microbiome? Many published associations come from small studies, and different laboratories sometimes reach contradictory conclusions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The commercial market has moved faster than the science. Probiotic supplements, which contain live bacteria, are sold on the promise of improving health, yet for healthy people, rigorous trials show little benefit. Home tests that analyse a stool sample and offer personalised dietary advice rest on even weaker foundations, since there is no agreed definition of a healthy microbiome. Regulators in several countries have begun to challenge unsupported claims, though enforcement is uneven and the language of marketing often stays one step ahead of the rules. Consumers, meanwhile, are left to judge the claims largely alone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, there are grounds for cautious optimism. Researchers are developing treatments that target specific bacteria, and early trials of microbiome-based therapies for inflammatory bowel disease are encouraging. The most reliable advice for the present is unglamorous: eating a varied diet rich in fibre, and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics, is associated with a more diverse microbiome and better health. As often in medicine, the unspectacular advice is better supported than the spectacular promise.
